title: Watching a Superconducting Coplanar Waveguide Heat Up with a Single Color Center
authors: Ioannis Karapatzakis, Jeremias Resch, David Hunger, Wolfgang Wernsdorfer
abstract: Single color centers in diamond offer a local probe of their cryogenic environment, providing a direct way to quantify heating in spin-control hardware. Here, we establish a single spectrally stable tin-vacancy (SnV) center as an on-chip thermometer for a diamond membrane and use it to characterize microwave- and radio-frequency-induced heating in a superconducting coplanar waveguide patterned on the same chip. We first calibrate the temperature dependence of the optical C-transition frequency and linewidth from $20\,\mathrm{K}$ down to the few-kelvin regime. At lower temperatures, where the optical response becomes weakly temperature dependent, we use the spin-lattice relaxation time $T_1$ as a complementary thermometer and tune its sensitivity with the transverse magnetic-field component. Applying this local thermometer to a niobium coplanar waveguide, we observe magnetic-field-dependent superconducting breakdown under GHz drive, accompanied by abrupt heating of the diamond. In contrast, at $20\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and $400\,\mathrm{mT}$, relevant for nuclear-spin control, we detect no measurable heating up to the breakdown threshold of $9.4\,\mathrm{dBm}$, corresponding to $B_\mathrm{ac}\sim1.2\,\mathrm{mT}$. These results define a safe operating window for superconducting microwave and RF control structures in diamond-based quantum nodes.
summary: The research develops an on-chip thermometer using single $	ext{SnV}$ color centers to measure local temperature changes within superconducting waveguides. By monitoring optical and spin properties, the authors characterize how MW/RF driving induces heating, ultimately defining safe operational power limits crucial for building reliable quantum network nodes.
main_problem: The primary goal is quantifying local heating effects induced by microwave (MW) or radio-frequency (RF) control fields in superconducting coplanar waveguides patterned on diamond substrates.
main_result: The study defines a safe operating window for such structures, showing that at relevant RF frequencies and magnetic fields, no measurable heating occurs up to high power thresholds, unlike MW driving which causes abrupt breakdown.
method: A local thermometer based on single color centers ($	ext{SnV}$) in diamond is used. Temperature is inferred by monitoring the spectral shift and linewidth of optical transitions, supplemented by spin-lattice relaxation time ($T_1$) measurements.
model_or_system: The platform consists of a superconducting Niobium (Nb) coplanar waveguide patterned on a diamond membrane hosting $	ext{SnV}$ color centers. Temperature calibration uses both optical spectroscopy and $T_1$ measurements across cryogenic temperatures.
key_observables: $	ext{SnV}$ C-transition frequency/linewidth, electron spin $T_1$ relaxation time, superconducting breakdown threshold ($P_{	ext{crit}}$), and thermal relaxation time ($	au_{th}$).
important_parameters: Temperatures ranging from 20 K down to the few-kelvin regime; magnetic fields up to 400 mT; input powers in the $10 	ext{ dBm}$ range.
main_assumptions: The linewidth is assumed to be a more reliable thermometer than the lineshift at very low temperatures. The slow thermal recovery time ($	au_{th}$) is attributed primarily to the adhesive layer rather than the diamond bulk.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $	ext{SnV}$ spectral shifts vs. temperature (Fig. 1, 2), schematic setups showing defect orientation relative to waveguides (Fig. 3), and power-dependent measurements of $T_1$ or fluorescence recovery time ($	au_{th}$) during pulsed driving.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the local thermometer using $	ext{SnV}$ spectroscopy across temperature regimes, applies this probe to measure heating from superconducting waveguides under varying MW/RF conditions, and concludes by defining safe operational limits for quantum control structures.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering challenge in solid-state quantum computing: maintaining stable cryogenic temperatures while applying high-power microwave signals necessary for qubit manipulation or readout.
